data.content_ref: inline:The target claims to avoid induction by replacing 'the theory will probably work' with 'the theory will probably generate fast learning,' but this replacement does not eliminate the inductive structure—it merely changes the predicate over which induction is performed. The target's mechanism bridges from past performance ('has withstood the most severe tests') to future epistemic yield ('maximizing the objective chance of learning from future errors') without any non-inductive justification for that bridge. If induction is illegitimate when it connects past survival to future truth (as the target insists), it is equally illegitimate when it connects past survival to future testability or learnability. The target's own countercondition 3 correctly identifies that relying on past performance to predict future practical success 'surreptitiously relies on inductive assumptions about nature's uniformity,' but the target fails to recognize that its own mechanism commits the identical fallacy with respect to the theory's future capacity to expose errors. A theory that was maximally testable and highly corroborated yesterday has, on strictly Popperian anti-inductive grounds, no guaranteed connection to being testable or informative tomorrow. The 'objective chance of learning from future errors' is therefore not objective at all—it is an inductive projection from past testability to future testability, smuggled in through the vocabulary of 'conventionalist decision' without the logical work being done.
